title: A High Priest Gets Clean Clothes
overview: In a vision, Joshua the high priest stands accused in God's court, has his filthy clothes replaced with clean ones, and hears promises about a coming servant called the Branch.

parts.label: The accuser is silenced (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Joshua, chief priest of the people newly returned from exile in Babylon, stands in a kind of heavenly courtroom, and Satan (a Hebrew word meaning "the accuser") stands beside him like a prosecutor. The LORD shuts the case down, not by denying any guilt but by pointing out that Jerusalem is chosen and Joshua is like a half-burned stick just pulled from the fire of exile.

parts.label: Filthy clothes swapped (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: The high priest was meant to wear splendid robes, so filthy clothes picture the sin and shame clinging to the priests and the people they represent. The angel has them removed and declares Joshua's sin taken away, and Zechariah himself asks for a clean turban, the priest's headdress that in the law carried the words "Holy to the LORD."

parts.label: A charge with a condition (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Being cleaned up comes with an expectation: if Joshua walks in God's ways, he will run the temple and guard its courtyards. He is also promised access among the heavenly attendants standing there, meaning a place close to God's presence.

parts.label: The Branch and the stone (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: "Branch" was a name earlier prophets used for a coming king from David's family, and Joshua and his fellow priests are called a sign that he is on the way; some think Zechariah's hearers would have thought of Zerubbabel, the governor from David's line, while Christians read the Branch as Jesus. The stone with seven eyes is unclear, possibly a temple building stone or a jewel for the priest's clothing, with the eyes often taken to mean God's full, watchful care, ending in a promise to remove the land's guilt in one day.

parts.label: Peace under the vine (v. 10)
parts.note: Sitting under your own vine and fig tree was a familiar picture of safety and plenty in ancient Israel. Here it describes the calm, neighborly life that follows once the guilt is gone.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this vision is mainly about restoring the priesthood and people in Zechariah's own day, with Jesus as a later fulfillment, or whether it is chiefly a direct prophecy of Jesus from the start.
think: When someone carries a past they cannot undo, what do you think actually makes a fresh start possible?
